science.title: Recent Developments in the National Implementation of Biological Weapons Convention: What Happened Since Resolution 1540?
science.description: This article examines the national implementation of the Biological Weapons Convention (BWC), focusing on the enactment of penal legislation to prohibit biological weapons in accordance with Article IV of the BWC and contrasting it with obligations under UN Security Council Resolution 1540. While there has been a significant increase in states adopting biological weapons-related penal laws since the adoption of Resolution 1540 in 2004, much of this legislation addresses biological weapons primarily within a terrorism context, limiting its scope compared to the broader prohibitions required by Article IV BWC. The article highlights that Resolution 1540's binding nature and the active facilitation role of the 1540 Committee have contributed to increased legislative adoption, but this focus on terrorism may inadvertently create gaps in comprehensive biological weapons prohibition. It suggests that lessons from Resolution 1540's implementation, including enhanced support mechanisms like the BWC's Implementation Support Unit, could improve broader national compliance with the BWC's obligations.

science.title: (015) STOMP: Sexual function Trial of Overactive bladder: Medication versus PTNS.
science.description: This article focuses on a study comparing the effects of percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS) and medical therapy (MT) using anticholinergics (ACH) or beta-agonists (BAG) on female sexual function in women with overactive bladder (OAB). The prospective multi-center cohort study measured sexual function using the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) before and after 12 weeks of treatment. Results showed that while both PTNS and MT improved OAB symptoms, ACH was associated with worsening sexual arousal, whereas BAG improved overall sexual function and pain, particularly in postmenopausal women. These findings contribute to understanding how different OAB treatments impact female sexual function and may inform patient treatment choices.

science.title: A Qualitative Exploration of First-Generation Asian Immigrants' Financial Behaviors in the United States.
science.description: Although Asians are one of the fastest-growing immigrant groups in the United States, their financial behaviors remain largely understudied. The purpose of the study was to understand Asian immigrants' lived experiences of financial behaviors and integration postmigration to the United States. Phenomenological inquiry, using semistructured, one-on-one interviews, was conducted with a convenience sample of 13 first-generation Asian immigrants in a medium-sized Midwestern city. Four themes were constructed from the thematic analysis: (a) spending behavior, (b) perception of debt, (c) utilization of support, and (d) savings. Specifically, we found that despite being highly educated and motivated, all participants experienced challenges with the financial system and institutions postmigration. To overcome these barriers, participants utilized informal support, such as family and friends, instead of formal support in navigating the financial system. Participants also reflected on how their Asian immigrant background influenced their financial behaviors, such as engaging in self-control when spending, maintaining an aversion to debt, and saving money for the future. Recommendations for culturally appropriate financial educational programming, as well as nonrestrictive policies for loans and credit for new immigrants, are advised so that financial professionals can support the full financial integration of the growing Asian immigrant community.
